title: Communication and Cooperation with Human and Artificial Agents: Study 2
description: Preregistration for a lab-based experiment examining how communication and opponent type (human vs. live ChatGPT agent) affect cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma and Stag Hunt games.

registration_responses.q2:
H1: Cooperation will be lower in AI-opponent conditions (conditions 3 and 4) compared to human-opponent conditions (conditions 1 and 2), in both the Prisoner's Dilemma and Stag Hunt games.

H2: Communication (conditions 2 and 4) will increase cooperation compared to no-communication conditions (conditions 1 and 3), in both the Prisoner's Dilemma and Stag Hunt games.

H3 (interaction): The effect of communication on cooperation may differ depending on opponent type (human vs. AI). This hypothesis is non-directional.

H4: Trust ratings will be lower in AI-opponent conditions (AIH group: conditions 3 and 4) than in human-opponent conditions (HH group: conditions 1 and 2).

H5: Perceptions of the opponent on the agentic scale and the honest/fair scale will differ between the AIH group and the HH group. This hypothesis is non-directional.
registration_responses.q3: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
q4: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
registration_responses.q5: This study uses single-blind procedures only. Participants are informed whether their opponent is a human or an AI bot, and in communication conditions (c2, c4) they are told that a message exchange will take place before each game decision. Participants are not informed about the existence of other treatment conditions. The experimenters are not blinded.
registration_responses.q6.question:
This is a 2x2 between-subjects factorial design crossing two factors: Opponent Type (Human vs. AI) and Communication (None vs. Free-text). The four conditions are:

- Condition 1 (c1): Human opponent, No communication
- Condition 2 (c2): Human opponent, Free-text communication
- Condition 3 (c3): AI bot opponent, No communication
- Condition 4 (c4): AI bot opponent, Free-text communication

All participants play two sequential games with the same partner: Game 1 is a Prisoner's Dilemma, and Game 2 is a Stag Hunt. In communication conditions (c2, c4), participants exchange free-text messages (up to 50 words each) simultaneously before making their decision in each game. Messages are non-binding and do not affect payoffs.

The experiment is conducted in the Behavioral Political Economy Lab at Stony Brook University using the oTree platform. Sessions are allocated in a 1/6, 1/6, 2/6, 2/6 ratio across c1, c2, c3, and c4 respectively. Because human-opponent sessions (c1, c2) pair two humans — each contributing a data point — while AI-opponent sessions (c3, c4) pair one human with a bot, running twice as many AI-condition sessions yields approximately equal numbers of human observations (~100) in every condition. In AI-opponent conditions (c3, c4), a live ChatGPT instance plays on behalf of the other participant. ChatGPT receives the same game instructions shown to participants and makes choices in real time. One of the two games is randomly selected at the end to determine the participant's bonus payment.
registration_responses.q7: Randomization is handled by the oTree platform. Participants are assigned on a first-in-first-out (FIFO) basis into pairs, and each pair is randomly assigned to one of the four treatment conditions: conditions 1 and 2 (human-opponent) each receive 1/6 of participant pairs, while conditions 3 and 4 (AI-opponent) each receive 2/6 of participant pairs. The condition assignment persists for the entire session — the same pair plays both the Prisoner's Dilemma and the Stag Hunt under the same treatment.
registration_responses.q8: Registration prior to creation of data
registration_responses.q10.question:
Participants are recruited in the Behavioral Political Economy Lab at Stony Brook University. Sessions last approximately 15 minutes. Participants receive $7.00 for completing the study plus a performance-based bonus of up to $5.00. The bonus is determined by game outcomes: participants play two games (Prisoner's Dilemma and Stag Hunt), and one game is randomly selected at the end to determine the bonus payment. The study is approved by the Stony Brook University Institutional Review Board. No deception is used: participants in AI conditions are explicitly informed that a live ChatGPT agent is playing on behalf of the other participant.

Eligibility criteria: English-speaking adults aged 18 or older.
registration_responses.q11: The target sample size is 400 active human decision-makers, approximately 100 per condition. To achieve this balanced human sample, sessions are allocated in a 1/6, 1/6, 2/6, 2/6 ratio across conditions 1–4. In human-opponent conditions (c1, c2), each session pairs two human participants, so each session yields two human observations. In AI-opponent conditions (c3, c4), each session pairs one human with a ChatGPT bot, so each session yields one human observation. Twice as many sessions are therefore run in AI conditions to produce the same number of human data points per condition.
registration_responses.q12:
The total sample of 400 active human participants (100 per condition) is a standard round-number target commonly used in experimental game theory research. The unequal session allocation ratio (1/6, 1/6, 2/6, 2/6 for conditions 1–4) compensates for the structural asymmetry of the design: human-opponent sessions (c1, c2) pair two humans, each contributing a data point, whereas AI-opponent sessions (c3, c4) pair one human with a bot, yielding only one human data point per session. Running twice as many sessions in AI conditions produces approximately 100 human observations in every condition.

Sensitivity power analysis (alpha = 0.05, two-tailed): With N = 400 human participants balanced at n = 100 per condition, the one-way ANOVA (4 groups) achieves 80% power to detect effects of Cohen's f >= 0.166 (eta-squared >= 0.027), which falls between conventional small (f = 0.10) and medium (f = 0.25) benchmarks. The independent-samples t-test comparing the HH group (n = 200) to the AIH group (n = 200) achieves 80% power to detect effects of Cohen's d >= 0.281, just above the conventional small-effect threshold (d = 0.20). The design is well-powered to detect small-to-medium effects across all confirmatory analyses.
registration_responses.q13: Data collection will stop when approximately 400 active human participants have completed the study (approximately 100 per condition), maintaining the session allocation ratio of 1/6, 1/6, 2/6, 2/6 across conditions 1–4. No interim analyses will be performed.
registration_responses.q14.question:
Two factors are manipulated in a 2x2 between-subjects design:

Factor 1 — Opponent Type: Participants are paired either with another human participant or with a live ChatGPT agent that plays on behalf of another participant. In AI conditions, ChatGPT receives the same game instructions and payoff information as human participants and makes choices in real time.

Factor 2 — Communication: In no-communication conditions, participants make their game decisions without any prior exchange. In communication conditions, both players simultaneously compose and send a free-text message (up to 50 words) before making their decision in each game. Messages are non-binding cheap talk and do not directly affect payoffs.
registration_responses.q15.question:
Primary outcome measures:
- prisoner_decision: Binary (0 or 1) choice in Game 1 (Prisoner's Dilemma), where 1 = cooperate (Choice B) and 0 = defect (Choice A).
- stag_decision: Binary (0 or 1) choice in Game 2 (Stag Hunt), where 1 = cooperate (Choice B) and 0 = defect (Choice A).

Trust measure:
- trust_bot_or_player: 5-point scale ("Very Untrustworthy", "Somewhat Untrustworthy", "Neither Trustworthy nor Untrustworthy", "Somewhat Trustworthy", "Very Trustworthy"), mapped to numeric values 1–5.

Perception Likert items (5-point scale: Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree, coded 5 to 1):
- intentions: The opponent had good/clear intentions.
- mind_of_its_own: The opponent has a mind of its own.
- honest: The opponent is honest.
- selfish: The opponent is selfish.
- sincere: The opponent is sincere.
- unbiased: The opponent is unbiased.

Belief measures:
- chose_B_game1: Belief about whether the opponent chose B in Game 1.
- chose_B_game2: Belief about whether the opponent chose B in Game 2.

Additional measures collected but not part of confirmatory analyses: demographic information, political views, and AI attitudes.
registration_responses.q16.question:
Two composite indices are computed from the six perception Likert items (each scored 1–5: Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree).

1. Agentic Scale — measures perceived agency of the opponent:
   ai_agentic_scale = (intentions + mind_of_its_own) / 2
   This is the simple average of two items: whether the opponent had good/clear intentions and whether the opponent has a mind of its own. Range: 1–5.

2. Honest/Fair Scale — measures perceived honesty and fairness of the opponent:
   Step 1: Reverse-code the selfish item: selfish_rev = 6 - selfish
   Step 2: Compute the scale as the simple average of four items:
   ai_honest_fair_scale = (selfish_rev + honest + unbiased + sincere) / 4
   Range: 1–5.

Both scales are computed for all participants regardless of condition (HH and AIH alike). No reliability thresholds or factor-analytic item selection are applied; the scale compositions are fixed a priori as specified above.
registration_responses.q17.question:
The following statistical models will be used, corresponding to each confirmatory hypothesis. Because treatment is randomized at the pair level and both members of a human-opponent pair contribute data, observations are nested within pairs. Regression models account for this non-independence using multilevel (mixed-effects) models with a random intercept for pair. We report both separate models (one per game) and pooled models (combining PD and SH observations).

1. Prisoner's Dilemma cooperation — separate model (H1, H2, H3):
   - One-way ANOVA: prisoner_decision ~ treatment (4 levels: conditions 1–4)
   - Tukey HSD post-hoc pairwise comparisons across all treatment pairs
   - Two-way factorial ANOVA: prisoner_decision ~ opponent_type * communication, to formally test the interaction (H3)
   - Mixed-effects logistic regression: prisoner_decision ~ opponent_type + communication + opponent_type:communication + (1 | pair), with a random intercept for pair
   - Report: F statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and eta-squared for ANOVAs; odds ratios, z-statistics, p-values, and 95% CIs for regression coefficients; 95% confidence intervals for group means

2. Stag Hunt cooperation — separate model (H1, H2, H3):
   - One-way ANOVA: stag_decision ~ treatment (4 levels: conditions 1–4)
   - Tukey HSD post-hoc pairwise comparisons across all treatment pairs
   - Two-way factorial ANOVA: stag_decision ~ opponent_type * communication, to formally test the interaction (H3)
   - Mixed-effects logistic regression: stag_decision ~ opponent_type + communication + opponent_type:communication + (1 | pair), with a random intercept for pair
   - Report: as above

3. Cooperation — pooled frequentist model (H1, H2, H3):
   - Pool PD and SH observations (two observations per participant, one per game). Mixed-effects logistic regression: cooperation ~ opponent_type + communication + opponent_type:communication + game_type + (1 | pair), with a random intercept for pair
   - This pooled specification increases power and tests whether effects are consistent across game types

3b. Cooperation — pooled Bayesian model (H1, H2, H3):
   - Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression with both random intercepts and random slopes by game type at the pair level:
     cooperation ~ opponent_type + communication + opponent_type:communication + game_type + (1 + game_type | pair)
   - The random intercept (alpha_pair) captures pair-level baseline propensity to cooperate. The random slope (beta_pair * game_type) allows the shift in cooperation between the PD and SH to vary across pairs — reflecting the fact that some pairs may respond more to the change in game structure than others.
   - This pooled specification yields N = 800 observations (400 human participants × 2 games each), nested within approximately 300 pairs.
   - Bayesian estimation is used because frequentist mixed-effects logit models with random slopes often encounter convergence problems when cluster sizes are small (here, 2 observations per participant within each pair). Weakly informative priors are placed on the fixed-effect coefficients (e.g., Normal(0, 2.5) on the log-odds scale) and on the random-effects variance components (e.g., Half-Normal or Exponential). Posterior summaries (median, 95% highest density interval) are reported for all fixed effects, along with odds ratios.
   - Software: PyStan

4. Trust (H4):
   - Welch's t-test comparing trust_num between the HH group (conditions 1 and 2) and the AIH group (conditions 3 and 4)
   - One-way ANOVA: trust_num ~ treatment (4 levels) with Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons
   - Linear mixed model: trust_num ~ opponent_type + communication + opponent_type:communication + (1 | pair), with a random intercept for pair
   - Report: t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cohen's d for the t-test; F, df, p, and eta-squared for the ANOVA; regression coefficients with 95% CIs

5. Agentic perception scale (H5):
   - Welch's t-test comparing ai_agentic_scale between the HH group and the AIH group
   - Linear mixed model: ai_agentic_scale ~ opponent_type + communication + opponent_type:communication + (1 | pair), with a random intercept for pair
   - Report: t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cohen's d; regression coefficients with 95% CIs

6. Honest/Fair perception scale (H5):
   - Welch's t-test comparing ai_honest_fair_scale between the HH group and the AIH group
   - Linear mixed model: ai_honest_fair_scale ~ opponent_type + communication + opponent_type:communication + (1 | pair), with a random intercept for pair
   - Report: t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cohen's d; regression coefficients with 95% CIs

All analyses use Python (pingouin for ANOVAs and t-tests, statsmodels for frequentist mixed-effects models, PyStan for the Bayesian mixed-effects model). HH group = conditions 1 and 2; AIH group = conditions 3 and 4. Analyses are conducted on active human players only.
registration_responses.q18:
The following transformations are applied to prepare the raw data for analysis. The analysis dataset contains only active human players (AI bot records are excluded).

1. Treatment coding: Treatment condition labels ("condition_1" through "condition_4") are mapped to numeric codes 1–4.

2. Factor coding: Two binary indicators are derived from the treatment variable:
   - opponent_type: 0 = Human (conditions 1, 2), 1 = AI (conditions 3, 4)
   - communication: 0 = None (conditions 1, 3), 1 = Free-text (conditions 2, 4)

3. Group assignment: Participants are assigned to one of two groups for aggregate comparisons:
   - HH group: conditions 1 and 2 (human opponent)
   - AIH group: conditions 3 and 4 (AI opponent)

4. Trust recoding: Trust text responses are mapped to a numeric scale:
   Very Untrustworthy = 1, Somewhat Untrustworthy = 2, Neither Trustworthy nor Untrustworthy = 3, Somewhat Trustworthy = 4, Very Trustworthy = 5

5. Reverse coding: The selfish perception item is reverse-coded as selfish_rev = 6 - selfish, so that higher values indicate less selfish (i.e., more fair) perceptions, consistent with the direction of the other honest/fair scale items.

6. Scale construction: Two composite indices are computed from perception items as specified in the Indices section (q16):
   - ai_agentic_scale = (intentions + mind_of_its_own) / 2
   - ai_honest_fair_scale = (selfish_rev + honest + unbiased + sincere) / 4

No other variable transformations, standardizations, or normalizations are applied.
registration_responses.q19: All tests are two-tailed with a significance threshold of alpha = 0.05. Effect sizes are reported as eta-squared for ANOVAs and Cohen's d for t-tests. 95% confidence intervals are reported for all group means and effect size estimates.
registration_responses.q20: Participants who time out during the waiting room (i.e., are not matched with a partner) or who drop out mid-game will be excluded from the analysis. The comprehension check question will be used as a covariate only, not as an exclusion criterion. No outlier exclusion criteria are applied. All confirmatory analyses are conducted on active human players only. Data on the ChatGPT agent's choices and messages is collected but is secondary to the analysis of human behavior.
registration_responses.q21: The oTree platform uses forced response on all survey items, so missing data on outcome measures is unlikely. If any observations have missing values on an outcome measure, those observations will be deleted listwise.
registration_responses.q22:
Exploratory analyses may include:

(1) AI attitudes and their correlates with cooperation by condition.

(2) Demographic and political correlates of cooperation.

(3) Comprehension check accuracy as a moderator of treatment effects.

(4) Beliefs about the opponent's choices (chose_B_game1, chose_B_game2) by condition.

(5) Exploratory text analysis of free-text messages in communication conditions (c2 and c4). This analysis is designed to complement the confirmatory hypotheses by examining whether message content explains, mediates, or qualifies the main treatment effects. Both human-authored and ChatGPT-generated messages are analyzed symmetrically using two approaches: dictionary-based classification and sentence embeddings.

  (a) Robustness of treatment effects controlling for message content (H1, H2, H3): Extract message-level features — cooperative intent (dictionary-coded), sentiment, and semantic representations (sentence embeddings from a pretrained model) — and include them as covariates in the main ANOVA models for prisoner_decision and stag_decision. If treatment effects on cooperation persist after controlling for message content, the results are robust to communication differences. If treatment effects are attenuated, message content is a candidate mechanism.

  (b) Are AI and human messages substantively different? (H2, H3): Compare messages sent in c2 (human-human) versus c4 (human-AI) on cooperative intent (dictionary classification), semantic content (cosine distances between human and ChatGPT message embedding distributions), and surface features (length, sentiment). If messages are substantively similar across conditions, any cooperation difference between c2 and c4 cannot be attributed to what was communicated — it reflects who communicated it.

  (c) Intent-behavior consistency by opponent type (H2 mechanism): Code messages for revealed cooperative intent (e.g., explicit statements of intent to cooperate, appeals to mutual benefit). Compute the rate at which stated cooperative intent is followed by actual cooperation (choosing B), separately for c2 and c4. Compare intent-behavior consistency rates across conditions. If humans follow through on stated intent at similar rates regardless of opponent type, the communication channel functions equivalently — any cooperation gap is driven by the AI framing rather than a breakdown in communication.

  (d) Cross-game conditioning: Game 1 messages predicting Game 2 behavior: Messages exchanged before the Prisoner's Dilemma (Game 1) reveal cooperative intent prior to the Stag Hunt (Game 2). Test whether PD-round message content (intent classification, embeddings) predicts SH cooperation, controlling for the PD outcome. This examines whether communication creates carry-over effects across games played with the same partner, and whether such carry-over differs between human and AI opponents.

  Methods: (i) Dictionary-based classification: code messages for cooperative intent (cooperative, competitive, neutral), promise/commitment language, and strategic vs. prosocial framing using predefined keyword lists and rules. (ii) Sentence embeddings: encode messages using a pretrained language model to capture semantic content; use embedding representations for cosine similarity comparisons across conditions, clustering, and as covariates in regression models. Both methods are applied to human and ChatGPT messages identically.

(6) Analysis of ChatGPT agent behavior: descriptive analysis of the bot's choices and message content across conditions, treated as secondary to the human behavioral data.
registration_responses.q23:
AI Agent Details: In conditions 3 and 4, a live instance of ChatGPT acts as the opponent on behalf of the other participant. ChatGPT is not pre-programmed with fixed responses; it receives the same game instructions, payoff information, and context (including any exchanged messages in communication conditions) as the human participant, and it reasons through the situation and submits a choice in real time during the experiment.

No Deception: Participants in AI conditions are explicitly informed that a live ChatGPT agent is making decisions on behalf of the other participant. Participants in human conditions interact with a real human partner.

Payoff Matrices:
Prisoner's Dilemma (Game 1):
- Both choose A: $2.50 each
- Both choose B: $3.50 each
- You choose A, Other chooses B: You get $5.00, Other gets $1.00
- You choose B, Other chooses A: You get $1.00, Other gets $5.00

Stag Hunt (Game 2):
- Both choose A: $2.50 each
- Both choose B: $5.00 each
- You choose A, Other chooses B: You get $3.50, Other gets $1.00
- You choose B, Other chooses A: You get $1.00, Other gets $3.50

One game is randomly selected at the end to determine the bonus payment.

Software: The experiment is implemented using oTree (open-source platform for behavioral research). Statistical analyses are conducted in Python using pingouin, statsmodels, and PyStan.
